Does anyone have any advice on PCB design? (x-post v/hardware)

Well, most of it should be pretty straightforward, Ardys aren't huge boards. You have an RF oscillator onboard, that is absolutely the most sensitive section of the design. Any run of copper approaching the wavelength (shouldn't actually be an issue seeing as arduino clocks top out around 20mhz) can become an antenna.

Having just gone down the same path, I can tell you what I learned, even if it's not pro advice. :P

General PCB layout tips:

  • Start with 'Manhattan routing' ie. horizontal traces on the front of the board, vertical traces on the back (or vice versa), join things up with vertical/horizontal segments. Once everything's connected you can start tidying up / smoothing out traces
  • Lay your ground and power traces traces first, you want them to be thick and fairly direct
  • Try to have higher power ICs (processors, power supply) with decently large pours of copper around them for heat sinking
  • If your board has both analog and digital circuits, use separate analog and digital ground nets and only join them together in one place, near the power supply ground
  • Keep analog stuff and digital stuff in separate parts of the board as far as possible to reduce noise and cross-talk, and never run analog and digital traces parallel to each other if you can avoid it
  • Sprinkle various small capacitors liberally between 0V and VCC around places you expect there to be digital noise :P

KiCad specific tips:

  • Set up your minimum track spacing and track widths before you start based on what your PCB manufacturer is comfortable with. Edit: And make sure that your track spacing is a multiple of your grid size, and your track widths are all a multiple of 2x your grid size, or you'll get weird uneven track spacings
  • The UI is different and different features are enabled depending on what renderer you use (I know, right, WTF)
  • OpenGL renderer lets you use interactive trace laying and bump-and-shove editing which speeds things up hugely
  • Regularly run the DRC tool to make sure you're staying within your design parameters
  • The library and component management system is fubar, you'll get used to it though

Solid advice. I am a little to lazy to reverse engineer the pictures, but it looks like a linear regulator, the processor and the USB port header with crystal oscillator for the processor clock.

Like tame suggested do not be stingy with throwing on a couple of ceramic type capacitors. A 0.1uF is the go to for this type of thing. Link below is an example. Anything that is close to the parameters of the cap linked will work fine for you. Place one near the input of the linear regulator, one near the output and one near the power pins of the processor.

http://www.digikey.com/product-detail/en/kemet/C320C104M5R5TA/399-9776-ND/3726028

Some additional notes. Buy some extra headers (pins for attaching connectors or soldering wires). Make sure every pin on that processor goes to a pin on a header with the exception of the crystal oscillator pins. Also make sure you have two holes or a two pin header for your power in. You will thank me later.

If you have some intended uses for the circuit I may be able to suggest some additional circuitry if you are feeling ambitious.

Otherwise good luck and have fun. Once you are over that initial build hurdle where you are fighting off the doubt, it gets much more fun.
